summary: Defines managed objects for source routing and source routing transparent bridges, which join Token Ring segments. These bridges are also expected to implement the relevant groups of the Bridge MIB. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Some bridges let the sender decide the path through a maze. This memo lists the gauges for checking on those bridges.

subtitle: The SNMP counters and settings for watching and configuring source routing bridges.

tldr.problem: Bridges that use source route bridging needed a standard set of managed objects, and the earlier definition in the Bridge MIB (RFC 1286) had to track changes in the IEEE 802.5M SRT Addendum.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1525 defines a MIB with a per-port table of segment, bridge number, frame size, spanning tree explorer mode and traffic and discard counters, plus an optional port-pair group.
tldr.outcome: It was a standards-track RFC that replaced RFC 1286 and is now Historic.

today: RFC 1525 is Historic. It obsoleted RFC 1286, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: What the MIB Manages
sections.content:
RFC 1525 defines part of the Management Information Base (MIB) for TCP/IP network management. It covers source routing and source routing transparent (SRT) bridges, which connect Local Area Network segments below the network layer. Such bridges are also required to implement the relevant groups of the Bridge MIB (RFC 1493).

It supersedes the dot1dSr group published in the earlier Bridge MIB, RFC 1286. The changes mostly follow the IEEE 802.5M SRT Addendum to the IEEE 802.1D standard for MAC Bridges. The memo builds on the Internet Network Management Framework: the SMI (RFC 1155 and RFC 1212), MIB-II (RFC 1213) and SNMP (RFC 1157).
sections.plainLanguage: It is a list of dials and gauges for one kind of network bridge, so a person far away can read how it is doing and adjust it.

sections.title: Keeping the MIB Small
sections.content:
The authors tried to keep the MIB as simple as possible. They applied six rules to proposed objects: start small and add only as needed, require objects to be essential for fault or configuration management, consider evidence of current use, limit the total, exclude objects derivable from others, and avoid heavy instrumentation of critical sections (one counter per critical section per layer).

Several IEEE management objects were left out as redundant or not useful, such as LimitedBroadcastEnable, DiscardLackOfBuffers and the byte counters for forwarded frames.

The MIB assumes a bridge also implements the Bridge MIB and the system and interfaces groups of MIB-II. Each bridge port is tied to an interface, and the counters apply only to traffic of protocols that the entity actually bridges.
sections.plainLanguage: The makers added only the gauges that really matter and left out the ones nobody needs, so the control panel stays easy to read.

sections.title: The dot1dSr Port Table
sections.content:
The dot1dSr group describes a bridge's source-routing state. It is for source route and SRT bridges; a bridge without source routing does not implement it. Its main object is dot1dSrPortTable, with one entry per port, indexed by a port number from 1 to 65535.

Each entry holds settings and counters. The settings are HopCount (the maximum routing descriptors allowed in All Paths or Spanning Tree Explorer frames), LocalSegment, BridgeNum, TargetSegment, LargestFrame and STESpanMode. Segment numbers range from 0 through 4095 and bridge numbers from 0 through 15, and 65535 means none is assigned. LargestFrame accepts only 64 values defined by the IEEE 802.5M addendum, from 516 up to 65535, and an illegal value is not accepted.

A scalar object, dot1dSrBridgeLfMode, says whether the bridge uses the older 3 bit or newer 6 bit length negotiation field in its Routing Information Field.
sections.plainLanguage: For every plug on the bridge there is a row of settings, like which street it faces and the biggest box it can carry. 65535 is the code for not set yet.

sections.title: Counters and Explorer Frames
sections.content:
Each port counts the frames it handles by kind. Specifically routed frames (also called source routed frames), All Paths Explorer frames (also called All Routes Explorer) and Spanning Tree Explorer frames each have an in and an out counter.

Discard counters record why frames were dropped: an invalid adjacent segment in the routing descriptor, a duplicate segment identifier, or a Routing Information Field longer than the maximum route descriptor length. Two further counters track duplicate LAN IDs or tree errors, which helps find problems with older IBM Source Routing Bridges, and LAN ID mismatches.

dot1dSrPortSTESpanMode sets how a port treats Spanning Tree Explorer frames. With forced(3) it always accepts and propagates them; with disabled(2) it silently discards them; with auto-span(1) it follows the Spanning Tree Protocol port state and accepts them only in the forwarding state.
sections.plainLanguage: Each plug keeps a tally of the different kinds of scout messages it has seen and a second tally of the reasons it threw messages away. One switch decides whether it listens to the scouts at all.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 1286 and the Port-Pair Group
sections.content:
The memo lists eight changes from RFC 1286, made after feedback from IEEE 802.5M. The group was split out of the Bridge MIB into its own document, dot1dSrPortLargestFrame became an INTEGER to allow 64 values, the port index range became 1 to 65535, two counters were added, wording was clarified for the specifically routed and all routes explorer counters, a scalar for 3 bit or 6 bit length fields was added, and the port pair group was introduced.

The dot1dPortPair group is optional. Bridges that support the port-pair multiport model of the IEEE 802.5M addendum use it. It has a table size gauge and a table indexed by a low and a high port, each row holding a bridge number and a state of enabled(1), disabled(2) or invalid(3). Writing invalid(3) removes the entry. The Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors fixed the first list after the standards group gave advice. They moved it into its own paper, added a few counters, and added an optional extra table for a different bridge design.

viz.caption: WHERE THE SR BRIDGE OBJECTS SIT UNDER THE BRIDGE MIB

items.label: auto-span
items.desc: Follows the Spanning Tree Protocol port state; frames are accepted only when the port is forwarding.

items.label: disabled
items.desc: Spanning Tree Explorer frames are silently discarded.

items.label: forced
items.desc: Always accepts and propagates Spanning Tree Explorer frames.
